engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: The Fork
chess.body: A fork attacks two pieces simultaneously with one piece. Knight forks are the deadliest — they move in an L-shape and cannot be blocked. Look for squares your knight can reach that simultaneously attack king + queen, or rook + rook. Practice: set up NxC5+ forking king and rook. Classic beginner trap.

wisdom.title: Regulate Yourself First
wisdom.body: You cannot be a calm parent if you're running on stress, sleep debt, and financial anxiety. Your regulation is their regulation — babies co-regulate with caregivers. Deep breath before you pick her up. Shoulders down. Slow exhale. Your nervous system sets the tone for the room.

book.author: Daniel Kahneman
book.chapter: The Planning Fallacy: Why Every Project Takes Longer
book.lesson: Kahneman and Tversky proved that humans systematically underestimate how long tasks take and overestimate how much they'll accomplish. Why? We build plans based on the best-case scenario and ignore what happened on similar projects in the past (outside view). The fix: reference class forecasting. Before estimating a project's timeline, ask 'how long did similar projects actually take?' The answer from historical data is almost always longer than your optimistic internal estimate. The cure for the planning fallacy is disciplined use of the outside view.
book.key_quote: Your intuitive project estimate is probably optimistic by 50-200%. Add a buffer based on historical data, not hope.
book.action: For your next project, find 3 similar past projects. Average their actual completion time. Use that as your baseline estimate.
crux: Two systems: System 1 is fast, automatic, emotional. System 2 is slow, effortful, logical.
System 2 is lazy and endorses System 1's answers with minimal checking.
What you see is all there is (WYSIATI). The mind builds confident stories from whatever is available.
Anchoring: an irrelevant number moves your estimate. Knowing this does not stop it.
Availability: vivid and recent events feel probable. Frequency gets confused with memorability.
Representativeness beats base rates. People pick the plausible story over the likelier category.
Loss aversion: losses hurt roughly 2x as much as equivalent gains please.
Prospect theory: you evaluate from a reference point, not in absolutes. Framing changes the answer.
Overconfidence is the most consequential bias, and expertise increases it.
The illusion of validity: confidence tracks story coherence, not predictive accuracy.
Regression to the mean explains most 'turnarounds' and most 'losses of form'.
The planning fallacy: forecasts default to best-case. Use the outside view and comparable past cases.
The remembering self and the experiencing self disagree. Memory is dominated by peaks and endings.
Formulas beat expert intuition in noisy, low-validity environments. Checklists and algorithms win.
learnings: You cannot debias yourself by intention. You can build procedures that catch the bias.
Fluency masquerades as truth. Anything easy to process feels more likely.
Expert intuition is real only where feedback is fast and regular. Markets do not qualify.
Write the forecast down before the outcome, or hindsight will rewrite it.
examples: Israeli parole judges granted parole ~65% of the time right after a meal break and near 0% just before one. Same evidence, different glucose.
The Linda problem: most people rate 'bank teller and feminist' as likelier than 'bank teller', which is logically impossible.
Kahneman's flight-instructor insight: praise after a good flight seemed to hurt and criticism after a bad one seemed to help. It was regression to the mean, not feedback working.
adapt: Write the trade thesis before entry. Post-hoc explanation is System 1 inventing a story.
Use base rates on the Dubai search: what fraction of applications convert? Plan on that, not on the best case.
The planning fallacy is why estimates slip. Take the outside view — how long did the last comparable build actually take?
Backtest numbers over gut feel. -0.029R on 1H means the 1H feeling is wrong, however strong it is.

father.do: Hand her to grandparents, friends, and colleagues while you stay visible in the room.

interview_tech.q: What is the difference between an associate and a subsidiary in your accounts?
interview_tech.a: Control versus significant influence. A subsidiary is controlled — you consolidate line by line and recognise NCI. An associate is significant influence, presumed at 20–50%, accounted for using the equity method: one line on the balance sheet at cost plus your share of post-acquisition reserves, and one line in P&L for your share of profit. Nothing of the associate's revenue or EBITDA enters your group numbers — a point that catches people out when a joint-venture-heavy group reports headline growth.

interview_tech.q: Compare owned retail, franchise, and concession from a finance perspective.
interview_tech.a: Owned: full revenue, full margin, full capex, full lease and staffing risk. Franchise: you book a royalty and wholesale margin — far lower revenue, far lower risk, and no control over the customer experience. Concession: you occupy space inside a host retailer, pay a percentage of sales rather than fixed rent, so occupancy cost flexes with trading and downside is capped. In the Gulf, franchise is the dominant international-brand model, which is why groups like Alshaya and Al-Futtaim report differently from the brands they carry.

interview_soft.q: The board pushes back hard on your numbers in front of everyone. What do you do?
interview_soft.a: Do not defend and do not fold. Separate the challenge into fact and judgement. If they have spotted a factual error, concede immediately and precisely — 'you are right, that is the restated base, I will recirculate by Thursday.' Credibility survives errors; it does not survive defensiveness. If it is a judgement call, state your assumption, the sensitivity, and offer the alternative case. Never argue methodology in the room; take it offline with the one director who raised it.

interview_soft.q: An employee asks you to approve an expense that is within policy but clearly wrong. What now?
interview_soft.a: They are testing whether you hide behind rules. Policy is a floor, not a ceiling. Approve or reject on the substance, explain the reasoning to the person directly, and then fix the policy so the next person is not in the same position. If it involves a senior person, the answer does not change — that is precisely when it counts. Say plainly that you would escalate to the audit committee if pressured to approve something you believe is wrong.
interview_soft.who: Any group with a code of conduct

cfo_field.q: Read the cash flow statement first. Always.
cfo_field.a: P&L is an opinion, cash is a fact. Open any set of accounts at the cash flow statement, compare operating cash flow to EBITDA over three years, and look at the gap. A business converting 90%+ of EBITDA to operating cash is real. One converting 50% has its profit sitting in working capital or is capitalising something it should be expensing. That one ratio finds more problems than any variance pack.
cfo_field.who: The first thing to check, every time

cfo_field.q: Scenario planning beats a single budget, and costs less than it sounds.
cfo_field.a: Three cases — base, downside, upside — with the two or three variables that actually move the outcome, not thirty. In retail that is usually like-for-like growth, gross margin, and rent renewals. The value is not the numbers; it is that the board has already discussed the downside before it arrives, so the conversation when it does is about the response rather than about whether it is happening.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece development: stop moving the same pawn twice; aim to bring both knights out by move 4, saving ≈30 seconds per turn.
Focus on time management: allocate ~30 seconds per move early; practice quick, solid opening moves (e.g., 1…e5) to avoid 19‑move timeout.
lichess_games.standout: Decided on the clock, not the board — the position was still playable when time ran out.

lichess_summary.session_summary: You’re playing a textbook “no‑risk” game that never threatens anyone—zero wins, two losses, and no draws proves you’re either over‑cautious or clueless about the critical moments. Your opening repertoire is a complete disaster; you’re either dumping into the worst lines or refusing to fight for the center, so every opponent is already a step ahead before move 2. Stop avoiding complications, study the main‑line King’s Indian Defense (or the Sicilian Najdorf if you prefer sharp play), and force yourself into tactical positions where you can actually convert a mistake into a win.
